newsitem.title: UK: Cable suffers from dlr strength but stg/mark firms.
newsitem.headline: Cable suffers from dlr strength but stg/mark firms.

text.p: Sterling was struggling against the dollar in Europe after the U.S. currency's overnight rally across the board, but sterling/mark was holding firm, helped by the mark's overall softness.

With the currency market busy watching the dollar's performance and developments in European monetary union, the pound lacked factors of its own and was mostly being pulled around by the dollar, analysts said.

"Sterling's really riding on the back of the dollar, which has got a firmer tone... The RPI figures were not really of any concern to the market, although perhaps they should have been a little disturbing," said Brian Hilliard, chief economist at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull in London.
Britain's retail price index (RPI) data for May, announced earlier, showed rises of 0.4 percent month-on-month and 2.6 percent on the year, slightly above expected increases of 0.3 and 2.5 percent.

Sterling ticked up after the data but analysts said this appeared to be a knee-jerk reaction. The RPI had not done much to change the market's outlook on British interest rates, particularly since the Bank of England had raised key rates only last week, analysts said.
The pound was trading at 2.8150/60 marks and $1.6317/27 at 1151 GMT, compared with 2.8100/10 and $1.6365/75 in late European trade on Wednesday.
Chancellor Gordon Brown's annual Mansion House speech to London's financial community was scheduled for this evening.

The Financial Times reported that Brown's speech would include an announcement that the Bank of England and its new monetary committee would be held accountable if they fail to meet the inflation target. Analysts said such an announcement was unlikely to alarm the market.

"But it's a speech in which he can range widely over the whole area of economic policy, so he might give some hints about what he's thinking on the budget. Of interest will be whether he will add to the belief that some extra fiscal tightening is needed quickly," SocGen's Hilliard said.

Some said the pound was benefitting somewhat from optimism about European monetary union going ahead, as EU politicians and officials on Thursday expressed optimism about agreeing on a key pact to ensure budget stability after EMU.

"Sterling tends to catch a slight bid when the market is talking about a broad-based EMU, although it's a side-play more than anything else," said James Barty, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
